sceneNotes.en: It's morning and you bump into a friendly neighbour on the street who is in a hurry but stops to say hello.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour !

forms.text: Bonjour !

en.meaning: Hello!
en.note: Works all day until the evening; use "Bonsoir" after dark.
en.literal: good day

expressions.pronunciationNote: The French r is made at the back of the throat: bon-ZHOOR.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Comment allez-vous ?

forms.text: Comment allez-vous ?

en.meaning: How are you?
en.note: Polite "vous" form, good for someone you don't know yet.
en.literal: how go you

expressions.pronunciationNote: Link the sounds: "allez-vous" sounds like ah-lay-VOO.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je vais bien, merci.

forms.text: Je vais bien, merci.

en.meaning: I'm fine, thank you.
en.literal: I go well, thanks

expressions.pronunciationNote: "Bien" is one nasal sound, like "byan" without a clear n.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je m’appelle Sam.

forms.text: Je m’appelle Sam.

en.meaning: My name is Sam.
en.note: Replace "Sam" with your own name.
en.literal: I myself call Sam

expressions.pronunciationNote: Say zhuh ma-PELL; the "e" in "je" is very light.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Et vous, comment vous appelez-vous ?

forms.text: Et vous, comment vous appelez-vous ?

en.meaning: And you, what's your name?
en.note: Polite form for a neighbour you don't know yet.
en.literal: and you, how yourself call-you

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Enchanté !

forms.text: Enchanté !

en.meaning: Nice to meet you!
en.note: A woman can write "Enchantée"; it sounds the same.
en.literal: enchanted

expressions.pronunciationNote: The first sound is a nasal vowel: ahn-shahn-TAY.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Au revoir, bonne journée !

forms.text: Au revoir, bonne journée !

en.meaning: Goodbye, have a good day!
en.note: Very common way to end a short chat.
en.literal: to the seeing-again, good day

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ça va ?

forms.text: Ça va ?

en.meaning: How's it going?
en.note: Casual and very common; fine with neighbours once you know them a bit.
en.literal: it goes?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ?

forms.text: Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ?

en.meaning: I'm fine, thanks. And you?
en.note: Natural reply that hands the question back.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: À bientôt !

forms.text: À bientôt !

en.meaning: See you soon!
en.literal: to soon

titles.en: Ordering a Drink at a Café

sceneNotes.en: You sit down on a busy café terrace where a quick, friendly server comes over to take your order.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour, monsieur !

forms.text: Bonjour, monsieur !

en.meaning: Hello, sir!
en.note: Use "madame" for a woman. Adding monsieur or madame is polite with staff.

expressions.pronunciationNote: The "j" in Bonjour is soft, like the s in "measure".

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: I’d like a coffee, please.
en.note: In France, "un café" means a small, strong espresso.
en.literal: I would-like a coffee, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Voudrais ends in a short "eh" sound, and the final s is silent.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Avec du sucre ou sans sucre ?

forms.text: Avec du sucre ou sans sucre ?

en.meaning: With sugar or without sugar?
en.note: The server asks this quickly, so listen for "avec" and "sans".
en.literal: With some sugar or without sugar?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Sans is a nasal vowel, and you do not pronounce the n.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Sans sucre, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Sans sucre, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: Without sugar, please.
en.note: To choose the other option, say "Avec du sucre, s’il vous plaît."
en.literal: Without sugar, if it you pleases

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: L’addition, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: L’addition, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: The bill, please.
en.note: This is very common in cafés. Add a smile and it is not rude.
en.literal: The addition, if it you pleases

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci beaucoup !

forms.text: Merci beaucoup !

en.meaning: Thank you very much!
en.literal: Thanks a lot

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je peux avoir un café, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Je peux avoir un café, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Can I have a coffee, please?
en.note: A common alternative to "Je voudrais". It is slightly more casual.
en.literal: I can have a coffee, if it you pleases?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je vous dois combien ?

forms.text: Je vous dois combien ?

en.meaning: How much do I owe you?
en.note: Natural when paying at the counter or to the server.
en.literal: I you owe how-much?

sceneNotes.en: You are at a fruit stall in a French market, asking the vendor about prices per kilo and maybe getting a little surprise.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour, madame !

forms.text: Bonjour, madame !

en.meaning: Hello, madam!
en.note: Use monsieur for a male vendor. Greeting a vendor first is expected in France.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Bonjour: nasal 'on', soft 'j' like the s in 'measure'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Les fraises, c’est combien le kilo ?

forms.text: Les fraises, c’est combien le kilo ?

en.meaning: How much are the strawberries per kilo?
en.note: Swap in any fruit: les pommes, les cerises, les abricots.
en.literal: The strawberries, it's how much the kilo?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Fraises: the French 'r' is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Six euros le kilo, ma belle !

forms.text: Six euros le kilo, ma belle !

en.meaning: Six euros a kilo, my dear!
en.note: Vendors often use friendly words like ma belle or mon grand. Say it as 'see zeu-RO'.
en.literal: Six euros the kilo, my beautiful

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ah, c’est un peu cher.

forms.text: Ah, c’est un peu cher.

en.meaning: Oh, that's a bit expensive.
en.note: Softened with 'un peu', which sounds friendly rather than rude.
en.literal: Ah, it is a little expensive

expressions.pronunciationNote: Cher: 'ch' as in 'sh', then an open 'è' sound.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous pouvez faire cinq euros ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez faire cinq euros ?

en.meaning: Can you do five euros?
en.note: Bargaining is light at French markets; a polite try is fine.
en.literal: You can make five euros?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: D’accord, je les prends.

forms.text: D’accord, je les prends.

en.meaning: Okay, I'll take them.
en.note: Use 'je le prends' for one masculine item, 'je la prends' for feminine.
en.literal: Okay, I them take

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Non, merci, ce sera tout.

forms.text: Non, merci, ce sera tout.

en.meaning: No, thank you, that will be all.
en.note: Better for turning down an extra offer. To decline entirely, say 'Non, merci, pas aujourd’hui.'
en.literal: No, thanks, it will be all

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ça fait combien, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Ça fait combien, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: How much is that, please?
en.note: Handy when you point at something or want the total.
en.literal: That makes how much, please

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Oh là là, c’est cher !

forms.text: Oh là là, c’est cher !

en.meaning: Wow, that's expensive!
en.note: More casual and expressive; say it with a smile.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Très bien, je prends un kilo.

forms.text: Très bien, je prends un kilo.

en.meaning: Great, I'll take a kilo.
en.note: Useful for saying how much you want to buy.
en.literal: Very well, I take one kilo

sceneNotes.en: You are a visitor looking for the train station, and a passer-by gives you quick directions, so you need to ask them to repeat and slow down.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Excusez-moi, monsieur.

forms.text: Excusez-moi, monsieur.

en.meaning: Excuse me, sir.
en.note: Use "madame" for a woman. Say it before you ask your question.
en.literal: Excuse me, sir

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Où est la gare, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Où est la gare, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Where is the station, please?
en.literal: Where is the station, if it pleases you

expressions.pronunciationNote: The French "r" in "gare" is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Vous allez tout droit.

forms.text: Vous allez tout droit.

en.meaning: You go straight ahead.
en.note: The passer-by says it quickly, so it may sound like one blurred word.
en.literal: You go all straight

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Puis tournez à gauche au feu.

forms.text: Puis tournez à gauche au feu.

en.meaning: Then turn left at the traffic light.
en.note: "À droite" means "to the right".
en.literal: Then turn to left at the light

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: C’est loin d’ici ?

forms.text: C’est loin d’ici ?

en.meaning: Is it far from here?
en.note: Said with rising intonation, this is the normal everyday question form.
en.literal: It's far from here?

expressions.pronunciationNote: "Loin" has a nasal vowel, so do not pronounce a clear "n".

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Non, c’est à dix minutes à pied.

forms.text: Non, c’est à dix minutes à pied.

en.meaning: No, it's ten minutes on foot.
en.literal: No, it's at ten minutes on foot

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Pardon, vous pouvez répéter ?

forms.text: Pardon, vous pouvez répéter ?

en.meaning: Sorry, can you repeat that?
en.literal: Pardon, you can repeat?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Plus lentement, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Plus lentement, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: More slowly, please.
en.note: Use this when the person speaks too fast for you.
en.literal: More slowly, if it pleases you

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci beaucoup, bonne journée !

forms.text: Merci beaucoup, bonne journée !

en.meaning: Thank you very much, have a good day!
en.note: Matches the "Merci beaucoup !" and "bonne journée" formulas from earlier in the chapter.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Excusez-moi, madame.

forms.text: Excusez-moi, madame.

en.meaning: Excuse me, ma'am.
en.note: Feminine form of address, for speaking to a woman.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous parlez vite. Plus doucement ?

forms.text: Vous parlez vite. Plus doucement ?

en.meaning: You speak fast. Slower?
en.note: A natural, friendly alternative that explains why you are asking.
en.literal: You speak fast. More gently?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Il y a une gare près d’ici ?

forms.text: Il y a une gare près d’ici ?

en.meaning: Is there a station near here?
en.literal: There is a station near from here?

sceneNotes.en: You bump into a neighbour carrying shopping bags in the stairwell of your new building, and she turns out to be friendly and chatty.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je suis votre nouveau voisin.

forms.text: Je suis votre nouveau voisin.

en.meaning: I'm your new neighbour.
en.note: A woman would say "nouvelle voisine".
en.literal: I am your new neighbour

expressions.pronunciationNote: "voisin" sounds like vwah-ZAN, with a nasal ending.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bienvenue dans l’immeuble !

forms.text: Bienvenue dans l’immeuble !

en.meaning: Welcome to the building!
en.note: The neighbour says this warmly and may then invite you for tea later.
en.literal: welcome in the building

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous venez d’où ?

forms.text: Vous venez d’où ?

en.meaning: Where are you from?
en.note: Polite and common in everyday speech.
en.literal: you come from where

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je viens d’Espagne.

forms.text: Je viens d’Espagne.

en.meaning: I'm from Spain.
en.note: Swap in your own country. Use "du" for masculine countries (du Canada) and "des" for plural ones (des États-Unis).
en.literal: I come from Spain

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous parlez anglais ?

forms.text: Vous parlez anglais ?

en.meaning: Do you speak English?
en.note: Rising intonation turns the statement into a question.
en.literal: you speak English

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je parle un peu français.

forms.text: Je parle un peu français.

en.meaning: I speak a little French.
en.literal: I speak a little French

expressions.pronunciationNote: The French "r" in "parle" is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je peux vous aider avec vos sacs ?

forms.text: Je peux vous aider avec vos sacs ?

en.meaning: Can I help you with your bags?
en.note: A natural thing to say when the neighbour is carrying shopping.
en.literal: I can you help with your bags

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci, c’est très gentil !

forms.text: Merci, c’est très gentil !

en.meaning: Thank you, that's very kind!
en.note: Good for answering the tea invitation.
en.literal: thanks, it is very kind

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je suis votre nouvelle voisine.

forms.text: Je suis votre nouvelle voisine.

en.meaning: I'm your new neighbour. (feminine)
en.note: Feminine form for a woman speaking.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je viens d’emménager.

forms.text: Je viens d’emménager.

en.meaning: I've just moved in.
en.note: Works for any gender.
en.literal: I come to move in

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous avez besoin d’un coup de main ?

forms.text: Vous avez besoin d’un coup de main ?

en.meaning: Do you need a hand?
en.note: A more casual, idiomatic way to offer help.
en.literal: you have need of a blow of hand

sceneNotes.en: You hail a taxi to the old town, the traffic is heavy, and the chatty driver quotes a price without using the meter.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour, vous êtes libre ?

forms.text: Bonjour, vous êtes libre ?

en.meaning: Hello, are you free?
en.note: Said at the taxi window or when you get in. Vous is used with a driver.
en.literal: Hello, you are free?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Libre: the French r is made at the back of the throat.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bonjour ! Où allez-vous ?

forms.text: Bonjour ! Où allez-vous ?

en.meaning: Hello! Where are you going?
en.literal: Hello! Where go you?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Dans la vieille ville, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Dans la vieille ville, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: To the old town, please.
en.note: Dans la vieille ville means 'into the old town'. You can also give the name of a street or square.
en.literal: In the old town, please

expressions.pronunciationNote: Vieille sounds like 'vyay', with a y sound at the end.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous pouvez mettre le compteur, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez mettre le compteur, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Can you put the meter on, please?
en.note: Use this when the driver quotes a price without the meter.
en.literal: You can put the meter, please?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Compteur: the p is silent in 'comp-', so it sounds like 'kon-teur'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ça va coûter combien, à peu près ?

forms.text: Ça va coûter combien, à peu près ?

en.meaning: About how much will it cost?
en.note: A natural way to ask for the fare before or during the ride.
en.literal: It will cost how much, roughly?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous pouvez vous arrêter ici, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez vous arrêter ici, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Can you stop here, please?
en.literal: You can yourself stop here, please?

expressions.pronunciationNote: Arrêter: the first part sounds like 'a-reh-tay'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous avez la monnaie sur un billet de vingt euros ?

forms.text: Vous avez la monnaie sur un billet de vingt euros ?

en.meaning: Do you have change for a twenty-euro note?
en.note: Avoir la monnaie sur... is the usual way to ask for change on a bill.
en.literal: You have the change on a note of twenty euros?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci, bonne journée !

forms.text: Merci, bonne journée !

en.meaning: Thanks, have a good day!
en.note: A standard polite goodbye when getting out of the taxi.
en.literal: Thanks, good day!

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous pouvez m’emmener dans la vieille ville ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez m’emmener dans la vieille ville ?

en.meaning: Can you take me to the old town?
en.note: Combines hailing the taxi and stating where you want to go.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Avec le compteur, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Avec le compteur, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: With the meter, please.
en.note: A shorter, still polite way to ask for the meter.
en.literal: With the meter, please.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ici, ça ira très bien, merci.

forms.text: Ici, ça ira très bien, merci.

en.meaning: Here is fine, thank you.
en.note: A relaxed way to say the spot is fine for dropping you off.
en.literal: Here, it will go very well, thanks.

sceneNotes.en: You are at the ice-cream cart outside the school with a child who wants a treat, but only two flavours are left and one scoop is the limit.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Je voudrais une glace, s’il te plaît !

forms.text: Je voudrais une glace, s’il te plaît !

en.meaning: I'd like an ice cream, please!
en.note: The child uses tu with the adult.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Glace: the 'a' is open, and the final 'ce' is a soft 's'.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vanille ou chocolat ?

forms.text: Vanille ou chocolat ?

en.meaning: Vanilla or chocolate?
en.note: Only two flavours are left.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Chocolat, s’il te plaît !

forms.text: Chocolat, s’il te plaît !

en.meaning: Chocolate, please!

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Une boule de chocolat, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Une boule de chocolat, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: One scoop of chocolate, please.
en.note: Said to the ice-cream seller, so it uses vous.
en.literal: one ball of chocolate, please

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Je peux avoir une deuxième boule ?

forms.text: Je peux avoir une deuxième boule ?

en.meaning: Can I have a second scoop?
en.note: The twist: the child asks for more.
en.literal: I can have a second ball?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Pas aujourd’hui, une seule boule, d’accord ?

forms.text: Pas aujourd’hui, une seule boule, d’accord ?

en.meaning: Not today, just one scoop, okay?
en.note: Soft and kind. The 'd’accord ?' at the end invites the child to agree.
en.literal: not today, one single scoop, okay?

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Oui, vas-y, mange ta glace !

forms.text: Oui, vas-y, mange ta glace !

en.meaning: Yes, go ahead, eat your ice cream!
en.note: Said once the child has accepted one scoop.
en.literal: yes, go there, eat your ice cream

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Mmm, elle est trop bonne !

forms.text: Mmm, elle est trop bonne !

en.meaning: Mmm, it's so good!
en.note: 'Elle' refers to the glace, which is feminine.
en.literal: she is too good

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Moi aussi, j’adore le chocolat !

forms.text: Moi aussi, j’adore le chocolat !

en.meaning: Me too, I love chocolate!

expressions.pronunciationNote: J’adore: the 'j' sounds like the 's' in 'measure'.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Merci, c’est gentil !

forms.text: Merci, c’est gentil !

en.meaning: Thanks, that's kind of you!
en.literal: thanks, it is kind

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: De rien !

forms.text: De rien !

en.meaning: You're welcome!
en.literal: of nothing

expressions.pronunciationNote: Rien: nasal vowel, 'ryan' without the final 'n' sound.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Une boule de vanille, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Une boule de vanille, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: One scoop of vanilla, please.
en.note: Alternative if the child picks vanilla.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Désolée, une seule boule !

forms.text: Désolée, une seule boule !

en.meaning: Sorry, just one scoop!
en.note: Feminine form, for a woman speaking. A man writes and says 'désolé' (same sound).

characters.name: Chloé

characters.name: Nadia

characters.name: Karim

sceneNotes.en: A lively bouchon, one of Lyon's small traditional restaurants, on a busy evening; the waiter is proud of the homemade quenelles.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bonsoir ! Vous êtes combien ?

forms.text: Bonsoir ! Vous êtes combien ?

en.meaning: Good evening! How many are you?
en.note: Bonsoir replaces bonjour from about 6 p.m. A bouchon is one of Lyon's small traditional restaurants; they fill up fast, so book ahead when you can.
en.literal: good-evening! you are how-many

expressions.pronunciationNote: Link vous and êtes: voo-ZET. Combien: kon-BYAN, both vowels nasal.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Une table pour deux, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Une table pour deux, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: A table for two, please.
en.note: Change the number: pour une personne, pour trois, pour quatre. Wait to be shown to a table rather than seating yourself.
en.literal: a table for two, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Deux: say 'duh' with rounded lips; the x is silent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Qu’est-ce que vous nous conseillez ?

forms.text: Qu’est-ce que vous nous conseillez ?

en.meaning: What do you recommend?
en.note: Conseiller (to advise) is the usual verb for this. Qu’est-ce que is the everyday way to start a 'what' question. Eating alone, say me instead of nous.
en.literal: what is-it that you to-us advise

expressions.pronunciationNote: Qu’est-ce que is just two beats: KESS-kuh. Conseillez: kon-say-YAY.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: La quenelle de brochet, elle est faite maison.

forms.text: La quenelle de brochet, elle est faite maison.

en.meaning: The pike quenelle, it's homemade.
en.note: A quenelle is a light, oven-baked pike dumpling, Lyon's signature dish. Naming the thing first, then picking it up with elle, is typical of spoken French. Fait maison = homemade.
en.literal: the quenelle of pike, she is made house

expressions.pronunciationNote: Quenelle: kuh-NELL. Brochet: bro-SHAY, with a silent t.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Qu’est-ce qu’il y a dedans ?

forms.text: Qu’est-ce qu’il y a dedans ?

en.meaning: What's in it?
en.note: Il y a = there is, there are; dedans = inside. For an allergy, ask: Il y a des fruits à coque dedans ? (nuts), du lait ? (milk), du gluten ?
en.literal: what is-it that it there has inside

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Du brochet, avec une sauce aux écrevisses.

forms.text: Du brochet, avec une sauce aux écrevisses.

en.meaning: Pike, with a crayfish sauce.
en.note: Du (de + le) means 'some': du brochet, du pain, du fromage. Aux (à + les) names a flavour or main ingredient: sauce aux écrevisses, tarte aux pommes.
en.literal: some pike, with a sauce to-the crayfish

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je vais prendre la quenelle, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Je vais prendre la quenelle, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: I'll have the quenelle, please.
en.note: Je vais prendre (I'm going to take) is the natural way to order. Swap in any dish: je vais prendre le plat du jour, the dish of the day.
en.literal: I go to-take the quenelle, if it you pleases

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Alors, ça vous a plu ?

forms.text: Alors, ça vous a plu ?

en.meaning: So, did you enjoy it?
en.note: Plaire works the other way round from 'to like': ça vous a plu = that pleased you. Waiters ask this as they clear the plates; you will also hear the shorter Ça a été ?
en.literal: so, that to-you has pleased

expressions.pronunciationNote: Plu has the French u: say 'ee' with tightly rounded lips.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Oui, c’était délicieux !

forms.text: Oui, c’était délicieux !

en.meaning: Yes, it was delicious!
en.note: C’était (it was) for a meal you have just finished; c’est délicieux while you are still eating. A simpler option: c’était très bon.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Délicieux: day-lee-SYUH; the x is silent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: On peut avoir l’addition, s’il vous plaît ?

forms.text: On peut avoir l’addition, s’il vous plaît ?

en.meaning: Can we have the bill, please?
en.note: On is everyday French for 'we'; its verb stays singular: on peut. The bill only comes when you ask for it. Service is included, so a tip is just a few coins if you were happy.
en.literal: one can have the addition, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Peut rhymes with deux: 'puh' with rounded lips, silent t.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous avez une table pour deux ?

forms.text: Vous avez une table pour deux ?

en.meaning: Do you have a table for two?
en.note: A statement said with a rising voice is the normal spoken question. Handy when you walk in without a reservation (sans réservation).
en.literal: you have a table for two

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Pour moi, le plat du jour, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Pour moi, le plat du jour, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: For me, the dish of the day, please.
en.note: Pour moi + the dish: the easiest way to order, no verb needed. The plat du jour is the daily special, usually the best value at lunchtime.
en.literal: for me, the dish of-the day, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Plat: plah, with a silent t. Jour: zhoor.

sceneNotes.en: A small clothes shop on the Presqu’île, Lyon's central shopping district; the assistant is attentive and the sizes run small.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bonjour ! Je peux vous aider ?

forms.text: Bonjour ! Je peux vous aider ?

en.meaning: Hello! Can I help you?
en.note: Always say bonjour when you walk into a French shop: skipping it comes across as rude.
en.literal: good-day! I can you help

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci, je regarde seulement.

forms.text: Merci, je regarde seulement.

en.meaning: Thanks, I'm just looking.
en.note: French has no separate '-ing' form: je regarde means both 'I look' and 'I'm looking'.
en.literal: thanks, I look only

expressions.pronunciationNote: Seulement: suhl-MAHN, ending on a nasal vowel with no n or t sound.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: En fait, je cherche un pull.

forms.text: En fait, je cherche un pull.

en.meaning: Actually, I'm looking for a sweater.
en.note: Chercher already means 'to look for': never add pour. Un pull is short for pull-over. False friend: actuellement means 'currently'; 'actually' is en fait.
en.literal: in fact, I seek a sweater

expressions.pronunciationNote: Pull has the French u (lips rounded, tongue forward): it does not sound like English 'pull'. The t of fait is usually silent.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bien sûr. Celui-ci est en taille S.

forms.text: Bien sûr. Celui-ci est en taille S.

en.meaning: Of course. This one is a size S.
en.note: Celui-ci = this one, for a masculine noun (celle-ci for a feminine one). French sizes often run small. Size letters are said the French way: S is 'ess', M is 'em', L is 'el'.
en.literal: well sure. this-one-here is in size S

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous l’avez en plus grand ?

forms.text: Vous l’avez en plus grand ?

en.meaning: Do you have it in a bigger size?
en.note: Plus grand = bigger; plus petit = smaller. L’ stands for le pull and goes before the verb: vous l’avez.
en.literal: you it have in more big

expressions.pronunciationNote: Plus here is 'plü' with a silent s; grand ends in a nasal vowel with a silent d: grahn.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Oui, voilà un M.

forms.text: Oui, voilà un M.

en.meaning: Yes, here's an M.
en.note: Voilà is what you hear whenever someone hands you something. To try it on, ask: Je peux l’essayer ? The fitting rooms are les cabines.
en.literal: yes, there-is an M

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Il coûte combien ?

forms.text: Il coûte combien ?

en.meaning: How much is it?
en.note: Il because pull is masculine; say elle coûte combien ? for a feminine item such as une veste (a jacket). The question word often comes last in spoken French.
en.literal: it costs how-much

expressions.pronunciationNote: Coûte: koot. The circumflex on û does not change the sound.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Quarante-neuf euros.

forms.text: Quarante-neuf euros.

en.meaning: Forty-nine euros.
en.note: The price on the tag is the price you pay: tax is always included in France.

expressions.pronunciationNote: kah-rahnt-NUHF uh-ROH: the f of neuf is pronounced, the s of euros is silent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Parfait, je le prends.

forms.text: Parfait, je le prends.

en.meaning: Perfect, I'll take it.
en.note: Le for a masculine item, la for a feminine one: je la prends. French uses the present tense where English says 'I'll take'.
en.literal: perfect, I it take

expressions.pronunciationNote: Prends: nasal 'an', silent d and s: prahn.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous prenez la carte ?

forms.text: Vous prenez la carte ?

en.meaning: Do you take cards?
en.note: La carte is short for la carte bancaire (bank card). Cash is en espèces, or du liquide. Small shops sometimes set a minimum for card payments.
en.literal: you take the card

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous l’avez dans une autre couleur ?

forms.text: Vous l’avez dans une autre couleur ?

en.meaning: Do you have it in another colour?
en.note: Couleur is feminine: une autre couleur. Colours go after the noun: un pull bleu, un pull noir, un pull rouge.
en.literal: you it have in an other colour

sceneNotes.en: The ticket office at Lyon Part-Dieu station on a busy afternoon; you and a friend want the next TGV to Marseille.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour, je voudrais un billet pour Marseille.

forms.text: Bonjour, je voudrais un billet pour Marseille.

en.meaning: Hello, I'd like a ticket to Marseille.
en.note: Pour gives the destination on a ticket: un billet pour Paris. Un billet is for trains and planes; un ticket is for the metro, bus or tram.
en.literal: good-day, I would-like a ticket for Marseille

expressions.pronunciationNote: Billet: bee-YAY (ll sounds like y, the t is silent). Marseille: mar-SAY, ending in a light y.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Un aller simple ou un aller-retour ?

forms.text: Un aller simple ou un aller-retour ?

en.meaning: A single or a return?
en.note: Aller = the trip out, retour = the trip back. You will see the same two words on the ticket machines.
en.literal: a going simple or a going-return

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Un aller-retour, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Un aller-retour, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: A return, please.
en.note: For a one-way trip, say: un aller simple, s’il vous plaît.
en.literal: a going-return, if it you pleases

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: À quelle heure part le prochain train ?

forms.text: À quelle heure part le prochain train ?

en.meaning: What time does the next train leave?
en.note: Partir = to leave; arriver = to arrive. After à quelle heure the verb comes before its subject: part le train.
en.literal: at what hour leaves the next train

expressions.pronunciationNote: The h of heure is silent, so quelle links to it: keh-LUHR. Train ends on the nasal vowel of vin, with no n sound.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Il part à quatorze heures dix, voie C.

forms.text: Il part à quatorze heures dix, voie C.

en.meaning: It leaves at 14:10, from platform C.
en.note: Timetables use the 24-hour clock: quatorze heures = 2 p.m. The minutes simply follow heures. Voie = platform (literally 'track'); at Part-Dieu the platforms have letters.
en.literal: it leaves at fourteen hours ten, track C

expressions.pronunciationNote: Link quatorze and heures: kah-tor-ZUHR. Dix is 'deess' at the end of a phrase.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Deux billets, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Deux billets, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: Two tickets, please.
en.note: The plural s is silent: billet and billets sound exactly the same. You hear the plural in the number or the article.

expressions.pronunciationNote: duh bee-YAY: the s of billets is silent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je dois descendre à quelle gare ?

forms.text: Je dois descendre à quelle gare ?

en.meaning: Which station do I have to get off at?
en.note: Devoir + infinitive = to have to: je dois descendre. Une gare is a railway station; un arrêt is a bus or tram stop; une station is for the metro.
en.literal: I must go-down at which station

expressions.pronunciationNote: Descendre: day-SAHN-druh (sc sounds like s). Dois: dwah.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: À Marseille Saint-Charles, c’est le terminus.

forms.text: À Marseille Saint-Charles, c’est le terminus.

en.meaning: At Marseille Saint-Charles, it's the last stop.
en.note: Saint-Charles is Marseille's main station. Le terminus is the end of the line: you cannot miss it.
en.literal: at Marseille Saint-Charles, it is the terminus

expressions.pronunciationNote: Saint-Charles: san-SHARL, with a silent final s. Terminus: tehr-mee-NÜSS, where the final s is pronounced.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je peux payer par carte ?

forms.text: Je peux payer par carte ?

en.meaning: Can I pay by card?
en.note: Par carte = by card; en espèces = in cash. Je peux + infinitive is the easy way to ask whether you may do something.
en.literal: I can pay by card

expressions.pronunciationNote: Payer: peh-YAY. Peux: 'puh' with rounded lips, silent x.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bien sûr. Ça fait quatre-vingt-seize euros.

forms.text: Bien sûr. Ça fait quatre-vingt-seize euros.

en.meaning: Of course. That comes to ninety-six euros.
en.note: Ça fait (that makes) announces a total. French builds 80 as quatre-vingts, 'four twenties', so 96 is four-twenty-sixteen. Belgian and Swiss French say nonante-six.
en.literal: well sure. that makes four-twenty-sixteen euros

expressions.pronunciationNote: kat-ruh-van-SEZ: vingt is a nasal 'van' with silent g and t.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Un aller simple pour Marseille, s’il vous plaît.

forms.text: Un aller simple pour Marseille, s’il vous plaît.

en.meaning: A single to Marseille, please.
en.note: No verb needed: naming what you want and adding s’il vous plaît is perfectly polite at a counter.
en.literal: a going simple for Marseille, if it you pleases

expressions.pronunciationNote: Simple: SAM-pluh, starting with a nasal vowel.

sceneNotes.en: On Place Bellecour on a hot afternoon, the friend you are walking with suddenly feels faint; a passer-by stops to help.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: S’il vous plaît, j’ai besoin d’aide !

forms.text: S’il vous plaît, j’ai besoin d’aide !

en.meaning: Please, I need help!
en.note: Avoir besoin de = to need (literally 'to have need of'). In an emergency in France, dial 15 for medical help (the SAMU) or 112, the European emergency number.
en.literal: if it you pleases, I have need of help

expressions.pronunciationNote: Besoin: buh-ZWAN, with a nasal ending. Aide sounds like 'ed'.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Qu’est-ce qui se passe ?

forms.text: Qu’est-ce qui se passe ?

en.meaning: What's going on?
en.note: Qu’est-ce qui (not que) because 'what' is the subject of the verb. Se passer = to happen.
en.literal: what is-it that itself passes

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Mon ami ne se sent pas bien.

forms.text: Mon ami ne se sent pas bien.

en.meaning: My friend isn't feeling well.
en.note: For a woman, write mon amie: it sounds the same, and it is still mon (not ma) before a vowel. Ne and pas wrap around se sent to make it negative.
en.literal: my friend not himself feels not well

expressions.pronunciationNote: Link mon and ami: mo-nah-MEE. Sent: 'sahn', nasal, with a silent t.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Il a très mal à la tête.

forms.text: Il a très mal à la tête.

en.meaning: He has a bad headache.
en.note: Avoir mal à + body part = to have a pain there: mal au ventre (stomach), mal au dos (back). For a woman: elle a très mal à la tête.
en.literal: he has very bad at the head

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Ne vous inquiétez pas. J’appelle le 15 ?

forms.text: Ne vous inquiétez pas. J’appelle le 15 ?

en.meaning: Don't worry. Shall I call 15?
en.note: The 15 (le quinze) is the SAMU, the emergency medical service. A present-tense statement said with a rising voice works as an offer: j’appelle ? = shall I call?
en.literal: not yourself worry not. I call the 15

expressions.pronunciationNote: Inquiétez: an-kyay-TAY, starting with a nasal vowel. 15 is quinze: kanz.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Non merci. Il y a une pharmacie par ici ?

forms.text: Non merci. Il y a une pharmacie par ici ?

en.meaning: No thanks. Is there a pharmacy around here?
en.note: Il y a = there is; par ici = around here. French pharmacists give advice on minor problems; look for the flashing green cross.
en.literal: no thanks. it there has a pharmacy by here

expressions.pronunciationNote: Pharmacie: far-mah-SEE. Il y a runs together: eel-YAH.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Oui, il y en a une juste en face.

forms.text: Oui, il y en a une juste en face.

en.meaning: Yes, there's one just across the street.
en.note: En stands for 'of them': il y en a une = there is one (of them). En face = opposite, across the street.
en.literal: yes, it there of-them has one just in face

expressions.pronunciationNote: eel-yahn-NAH ün: the n of en links to a.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: D’accord, j’ai compris. Merci pour votre aide !

forms.text: D’accord, j’ai compris. Merci pour votre aide !

en.meaning: OK, I've understood. Thank you for your help!
en.note: J’ai compris (I have understood) is the passé composé: avoir + past participle. Merci pour + noun: merci pour votre aide, merci pour tout.
en.literal: of agreement, I have understood. thanks for your help

expressions.pronunciationNote: Compris: kon-PREE, with a silent s.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous pouvez appeler un médecin ?

forms.text: Vous pouvez appeler un médecin ?

en.meaning: Can you call a doctor?
en.note: A doctor is un médecin; docteur is mostly a title, as in Bonjour, docteur. False friend: la médecine is the science; a medicine you take is un médicament.
en.literal: you can to-call a doctor

expressions.pronunciationNote: Médecin: mayd-SAN, two syllables, with a nasal ending.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Au secours !

forms.text: Au secours !

en.meaning: Help!
en.note: What you shout in real danger. À l’aide ! means the same.
en.literal: to-the rescue

sceneNotes.en: Your neighbour Martine has invited you to Sunday lunch with her family; she keeps filling your plate and wants to know all about your own family.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Entrez, entrez ! Faites comme chez vous.

forms.text: Entrez, entrez ! Faites comme chez vous.

en.meaning: Come in, come in! Make yourself at home.
en.note: Martine still says vous to you, and you to her: normal between neighbours until one of you suggests tu. Bring a small gift: flowers, chocolates or a bottle of wine.
en.literal: enter, enter! do as at-the-home-of you

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Votre gratin est vraiment très bon !

forms.text: Votre gratin est vraiment très bon !

en.meaning: Your gratin is really very good!
en.note: Bon (good) for food; bien is for how something is done. Gratin dauphinois, sliced potatoes baked in cream, comes from the Dauphiné, the region next door to Lyon.

expressions.pronunciationNote: Gratin: grah-TAN, with a nasal ending. Bon is one nasal vowel: no n sound.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Merci ! Et vous parlez très bien français !

forms.text: Merci ! Et vous parlez très bien français !

en.meaning: Thank you! And you speak French very well!
en.note: Bien (well) goes right after the verb, before the language: vous parlez bien français.
en.literal: thanks! and you speak very well French

expressions.pronunciationNote: Français: frahn-SEH; ç always sounds like s.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci, mais j’ai encore beaucoup à apprendre.

forms.text: Merci, mais j’ai encore beaucoup à apprendre.

en.meaning: Thank you, but I still have a lot to learn.
en.note: In France a compliment is often answered with a little modesty rather than a plain thank-you. Encore = still; beaucoup à + infinitive = a lot to (do).
en.literal: thanks, but I have still much to learn

expressions.pronunciationNote: Apprendre: ah-PRAHN-druh. Beaucoup: boh-KOO, with a silent p.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous avez des petits-enfants ?

forms.text: Vous avez des petits-enfants ?

en.meaning: Do you have grandchildren?
en.note: Petits-enfants (literally 'little children') = grandchildren; grandparents are grands-parents. Des cannot be dropped the way 'any' or 'some' can in English.
en.literal: you have some little-children

expressions.pronunciationNote: Three links in a row: voo-zah-VAY day puh-tee-zahn-FAHN.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Oui, deux ! Et vous, vous avez des frères et sœurs ?

forms.text: Oui, deux ! Et vous, vous avez des frères et sœurs ?

en.meaning: Yes, two! And you, do you have brothers and sisters?
en.note: Et vous ? hands a question back. French has no everyday word for 'siblings': you say frères et sœurs.
en.literal: yes, two! and you, you have some brothers and sisters

expressions.pronunciationNote: Sœur: like English 'sir' said with rounded lips. Frères: frehr, with a silent s.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: J’ai un grand frère et une petite sœur.

forms.text: J’ai un grand frère et une petite sœur.

en.meaning: I have an older brother and a younger sister.
en.note: Grand and petit also mean older and younger for brothers and sisters. Adjectives agree with the noun: un petit frère, une petite sœur.
en.literal: I have a big brother and a little sister

expressions.pronunciationNote: Petite: the second t is pronounced (puh-TEET) because of the final e; in petit it is silent.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Et vous restez longtemps à Lyon ?

forms.text: Et vous restez longtemps à Lyon ?

en.meaning: And are you staying long in Lyon?
en.note: False friend: rester means 'to stay', not 'to rest' (se reposer). À + city: à Lyon, à Paris.
en.literal: and you stay long-time at Lyon

expressions.pronunciationNote: Lyon: lee-ON, a nasal 'on' with no n sound. Longtemps: lon-TAHN.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je ne sais pas encore.

forms.text: Je ne sais pas encore.

en.meaning: I don't know yet.
en.note: Pas encore = not yet. In fast speech the ne is often dropped and you will hear something like 'shay pah'; keep ne and pas when you speak carefully.
en.literal: I not know not yet

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je suis fils unique.

forms.text: Je suis fils unique.

en.meaning: I'm an only child.
en.note: Fils unique (literally 'only son') for a man; a woman says fille unique. No article after je suis here.
en.literal: I am son only

expressions.pronunciationNote: Fils: feess (the l is silent, the s is pronounced). Unique: ü-NEEK.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: C’est un régal !

forms.text: C’est un régal !

en.meaning: It's a real treat!
en.note: A warm compliment on food that hosts love to hear. You can also say je me régale: I'm really enjoying this.

sceneNotes.en: Camille, whom you met in your first days, is now a friend, so you say tu to each other; she suggests the park on Saturday, but that day doesn't suit you.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Ça te dit d’aller au parc de la Tête d’Or samedi ?

forms.text: Ça te dit d’aller au parc de la Tête d’Or samedi ?

en.meaning: Do you fancy going to the Tête d’Or park on Saturday?
en.note: Ça te dit ? (does that say something to you?) = do you feel like it? The Parc de la Tête d’Or is Lyon's big park, with a lake and a free zoo. No word for 'on' before a day: samedi = on Saturday.
en.literal: that to-you says to go to-the park of the Head of-Gold Saturday

expressions.pronunciationNote: Tête d’Or: tet-DOR. Samedi: sam-DEE, two syllables.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Désolé, samedi je ne peux pas.

forms.text: Désolé, samedi je ne peux pas.

en.meaning: Sorry, I can't on Saturday.
en.note: A woman writes désolée; it sounds the same. With friends you say tu, but an apology like this one needs no 'you' at all.
en.literal: sorry, Saturday I not can not

expressions.pronunciationNote: Peux: 'puh' with rounded lips; the x is silent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Dimanche, ça te va ?

forms.text: Dimanche, ça te va ?

en.meaning: Does Sunday work for you?
en.note: Ça te va ? (does that go for you?) = does that suit you? To someone you say vous to: ça vous va ?
en.literal: Sunday, that to-you goes

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Oui, dimanche, ça marche !

forms.text: Oui, dimanche, ça marche !

en.meaning: Yes, Sunday works!
en.note: Ça marche (literally 'that walks') is the casual way to say 'that works' or 'OK, deal'.
en.literal: yes, Sunday, that walks

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: On fait un pique-nique ?

forms.text: On fait un pique-nique ?

en.meaning: Shall we have a picnic?
en.note: On + present tense, said with a rising voice, is how friends suggest something: on y va ? (shall we go?). French 'makes' a picnic: faire un pique-nique.
en.literal: one makes a picnic

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: On se retrouve à midi ?

forms.text: On se retrouve à midi ?

en.meaning: Shall we meet at noon?
en.note: Se retrouver = to meet up (literally 'to find each other again'). Midi is noon and minuit is midnight; neither takes heures.
en.literal: one each-other finds-again at midday

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Super ! Et après, on va boire un verre ?

forms.text: Super ! Et après, on va boire un verre ?

en.meaning: Great! And afterwards, shall we go for a drink?
en.note: Boire un verre (to drink a glass) = to go for a drink, whatever you order. Aller + infinitive: on va boire.
en.literal: super! and after, one goes to-drink a glass

expressions.pronunciationNote: Verre sounds just like vert (green): vehr.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Oui, avec plaisir !

forms.text: Oui, avec plaisir !

en.meaning: Yes, I'd love to!
en.note: Avec plaisir (with pleasure) works with friends and strangers alike. More casual still: carrément ! (totally!).
en.literal: yes, with pleasure

expressions.pronunciationNote: Plaisir: pleh-ZEER; an s between two vowels sounds like z.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Alors, à dimanche midi !

forms.text: Alors, à dimanche midi !

en.meaning: So, see you Sunday at noon!
en.note: À + a day or a time is how you say 'see you then': à dimanche, à demain (tomorrow), à ce soir (tonight).
en.literal: so, to Sunday midday

expressions.pronunciationNote: Alors: ah-LOR, with a silent s.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Et si on allait au cinéma ?

forms.text: Et si on allait au cinéma ?

en.meaning: How about going to the cinema?
en.note: Et si on + imperfect (allait) = 'what if we…?': a soft way to suggest something. Au = à + le. Friends often shorten cinéma to ciné.
en.literal: and if one was-going to-the cinema

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: C’est gentil, mais samedi je travaille.

forms.text: C’est gentil, mais samedi je travaille.

en.meaning: That's kind, but I'm working on Saturday.
en.note: Saying c’est gentil first softens the refusal. Je travaille is the present tense, used here for a fixed plan in the near future.
en.literal: it is kind, but Saturday I work

expressions.pronunciationNote: Travaille: trah-VAH-y. Gentil: zhahn-TEE, with a silent l.

notes: AI-assisted draft of chapter 3 for French (fr); native review required before publishing.

Tu between colleagues of the same level (Mathieu) and with friends (Léa, Hugo, and Camille, who returns from chapters 1 and 2); vous with the team lead Hélène at the first meeting and with Gérard, the café owner. Please confirm tu with a colleague in the first week feels natural.

The learner keeps the chapter-1 name Sam and the masculine default (fatigué, crevé, ravi, perdu, sorti); feminine forms are given in the notes. Sam's job, graphiste, is the same word for a man or a woman.
Wordings to check first: « dans la boîte », « Vous faites plutôt du print ou du web ? », « faire un point », « je suis fan de vélo », « Il était minuit. Enfin, onze heures, je veux dire. ».
Facts to verify: the Croix-Rousse market open every morning except Monday, metro C two stops from Hôtel de Ville to Croix-Rousse, the traboules of Vieux-Lyon.

characters.name: Mathieu
characters.personality: chatty, always first at the coffee machine, curious about how you are settling in

characters.name: Hélène
characters.personality: friendly and direct, talks fast and loves office jargon

characters.name: Léa
characters.personality: sporty, enthusiastic; a classmate from your Wednesday drawing class

characters.name: Gérard
characters.personality: café owner, born in Lyon, proud of the places tourists never find

characters.name: Hugo
characters.personality: good-humoured, loves a friendly argument, grew up in a Beaujolais village

characters.name: Camille
characters.personality: warm, cheerful, always in a rush; your friend from chapters 1 and 2, eager to hear your news

titles.en: A coffee break with a colleague

sceneNotes.en: The coffee machine at the design agency near Part-Dieu where you have just started; your colleague Mathieu wants to know how your days go.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Salut ! Alors, cette première semaine, ça se passe bien ?

forms.text: Salut ! Alors, cette première semaine, ça se passe bien ?

en.meaning: Hi! So, is your first week going well?
en.note: Colleagues of the same level usually say tu to each other in French offices. Ça se passe bien ? (is it going well?) works for a job, a trip or a meal.
en.literal: hi! so, this first week, that itself passes well

expressions.pronunciationNote: Semaine: suh-MEN. Ça se passe: sah suh PASS.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ça va, mais je suis un peu fatigué.

forms.text: Ça va, mais je suis un peu fatigué.

en.meaning: It's OK, but I'm a bit tired.
en.note: A woman writes fatiguée; it sounds the same. Un peu (a little) softens a complaint: un peu stressé, un peu perdu.
en.literal: that goes, but I am a little tired

expressions.pronunciationNote: Fatigué: fah-tee-GAY. Un peu: uhn PUH.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Ah bon ? Tu te lèves à quelle heure ?

forms.text: Ah bon ? Tu te lèves à quelle heure ?

en.meaning: Really? What time do you get up?
en.note: Se lever (to get up) is reflexive: je me lève, tu te lèves. Ah bon ? is the all-purpose 'really?' that keeps a chat going.
en.literal: ah good? you yourself raise at what hour

expressions.pronunciationNote: Lèves: lev. Quelle heure runs together: keh-LUHR.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je me lève à six heures et quart.

forms.text: Je me lève à six heures et quart.

en.meaning: I get up at a quarter past six.
en.note: Et quart = quarter past, et demie = half past, moins le quart = quarter to. In everyday talk people use the 12-hour clock: six heures du matin.
en.literal: I myself raise at six hours and quarter

expressions.pronunciationNote: Six heures links: see-ZUHR. Quart: kar, with a silent t.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je prends mon petit-déjeuner, puis le métro.

forms.text: Je prends mon petit-déjeuner, puis le métro.

en.meaning: I have breakfast, then I take the metro.
en.note: In France le déjeuner is lunch and le petit-déjeuner is breakfast (in Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec, déjeuner is breakfast). Prendre works for meals and transport alike.
en.literal: I take my little-lunch, then the metro

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Et tu fais quoi, exactement, dans la boîte ?

forms.text: Et tu fais quoi, exactement, dans la boîte ?

en.meaning: And what exactly do you do at the company?
en.note: Une boîte (a box) is everyday slang for a company: elle travaille dans une grosse boîte. Tu fais quoi ? is the casual 'what do you do?'.
en.literal: and you do what, exactly, in the box

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je suis graphiste, dans l’équipe d’Hélène.

forms.text: Je suis graphiste, dans l’équipe d’Hélène.

en.meaning: I'm a graphic designer, on Hélène's team.
en.note: No article before a job after je suis: je suis graphiste, never un graphiste. De becomes d’ before a vowel or a silent h: l’équipe d’Hélène.
en.literal: I am graphic-designer, in the team of Hélène

expressions.pronunciationNote: Graphiste: grah-FEEST. D’Hélène: day-LEN, the h is silent.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Et ce week-end, tu fais quelque chose ?

forms.text: Et ce week-end, tu fais quelque chose ?

en.meaning: And are you doing anything this weekend?
en.note: French borrowed week-end from English; Quebec says la fin de semaine. Ce week-end = this coming weekend.
en.literal: and this weekend, you do something

expressions.pronunciationNote: Week-end is said the French way, stressed at the end: wee-KEND.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Samedi, je vais faire la grasse matinée !

forms.text: Samedi, je vais faire la grasse matinée !

en.meaning: On Saturday, I'm going to sleep in!
en.note: Faire la grasse matinée (to do the fat morning) = to sleep in. Aller + infinitive is the near future: je vais faire, on va voir.
en.literal: Saturday, I go to-do the fat morning

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je suis crevé, mais ça va !

forms.text: Je suis crevé, mais ça va !

en.meaning: I'm exhausted, but I'm OK!
en.note: Crevé (literally 'punctured', like a tyre) is the casual word for exhausted; a woman writes crevée. Keep it for friends and colleagues.
en.literal: I am punctured, but that goes

sceneNotes.en: Your first meeting with Hélène, who leads your team at the agency and was away last week; she is friendly but talks fast and loves jargon.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Bonjour ! Hélène Garnier, je dirige l’équipe.

forms.text: Bonjour ! Hélène Garnier, je dirige l’équipe.

en.meaning: Hello! Hélène Garnier, I lead the team.
en.note: At work people often introduce themselves with first name and surname, then their role. Diriger une équipe = to lead a team.
en.literal: good-day! Hélène Garnier, I direct the team

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour, je me présente : Sam Taylor.

forms.text: Bonjour, je me présente : Sam Taylor.

en.meaning: Hello, let me introduce myself: Sam Taylor.
en.note: Je me présente (I present myself) is the formal way to give your name at work or in a meeting. In writing, French puts a space before a colon.
en.literal: good-day, I myself present: Sam Taylor

expressions.pronunciationNote: Présente: pray-ZAHNT; an s between two vowels sounds like z.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ravi de faire votre connaissance.

forms.text: Ravi de faire votre connaissance.

en.meaning: Pleased to meet you.
en.note: The formal 'pleased to meet you'. A woman writes ravie; it sounds the same. Lighter and very common: enchanté.
en.literal: delighted to make your acquaintance

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Vous faites plutôt du print ou du web ?

forms.text: Vous faites plutôt du print ou du web ?

en.meaning: Do you mostly do print or web?
en.note: Office French borrows many English words: le print (printed work), le web, un mail, une deadline. Plutôt = rather, mostly.
en.literal: you do rather some print or some web

expressions.pronunciationNote: Print is said almost as in English, with a French r: preent.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je fais surtout du web, mais aussi des affiches.

forms.text: Je fais surtout du web, mais aussi des affiches.

en.meaning: I mostly do web work, but posters too.
en.note: Faire du + field = to work in it: faire du web, faire du marketing. Surtout means 'mostly, above all', never 'surely'.
en.literal: I do above-all some web, but also some posters

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Très bien. On fait un point à quinze heures ?

forms.text: Très bien. On fait un point à quinze heures ?

en.meaning: Very good. Shall we have a catch-up at 3 p.m.?
en.note: Faire un point is office French for a short catch-up meeting. Work times use the 24-hour clock: quinze heures = 3 p.m.
en.literal: very well. one makes a point at fifteen hours

expressions.pronunciationNote: Point: pwan, a nasal vowel with no n or t sound. Quinze: kanz.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Pardon, que veut dire « faire un point » ?

forms.text: Pardon, que veut dire « faire un point » ?

en.meaning: Sorry, what does « faire un point » mean?
en.note: Que veut dire… ? or qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ? = what does … mean? Vouloir dire (to want to say) is how French says 'to mean'.
en.literal: sorry, what wants to-say « to-make a point »

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: C’est une courte réunion, pour voir où on en est.

forms.text: C’est une courte réunion, pour voir où on en est.

en.meaning: It's a short meeting to see where we're at.
en.note: False friend: une réunion is a meeting, not a reunion. Où on en est (where one of-it is) = how things stand.
en.literal: it is a short meeting, for to-see where one of-it is

expressions.pronunciationNote: Réunion: ray-ü-NYON. Où on en est: oo on-nahn-NAY.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: D’accord. Je dois préparer quelque chose ?

forms.text: D’accord. Je dois préparer quelque chose ?

en.meaning: OK. Do I need to prepare anything?
en.note: Devoir + infinitive = to have to: je dois préparer. A statement said with a rising voice is the simplest polite question.
en.literal: of agreement. I must to-prepare some thing

expressions.pronunciationNote: Préparer: pray-pah-RAY. Quelque chose: kel-kuh SHOHZ.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: En attendant, je peux m’installer ici ?

forms.text: En attendant, je peux m’installer ici ?

en.meaning: In the meantime, can I set up here?
en.note: S’installer = to settle in, to take a seat or a desk. Je peux… ? is the everyday way to ask permission; more formal: est-ce que je pourrais… ?
en.literal: in waiting, I can myself install here

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Bonjour, je suis Sam, le nouveau graphiste.

forms.text: Bonjour, je suis Sam, le nouveau graphiste.

en.meaning: Hello, I'm Sam, the new graphic designer.
en.note: Less formal and just as common. A woman says la nouvelle graphiste: the article and the adjective change, the job title does not.
en.literal: good-day, I am Sam, the new graphic-designer

titles.en: What do you do for fun?

sceneNotes.en: After your Wednesday evening drawing class at the local community centre, your classmate Léa asks what you do at weekends; it turns out you share a passion.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Et le week-end, tu fais quoi, en général ?

forms.text: Et le week-end, tu fais quoi, en général ?

en.meaning: And what do you usually do at weekends?
en.note: In casual French the question word often comes last: tu fais quoi ? En général = usually.
en.literal: and the weekend, you do what, in general

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Le samedi, je fais souvent du vélo.

forms.text: Le samedi, je fais souvent du vélo.

en.meaning: On Saturdays, I often go cycling.
en.note: Le samedi (with le) = on Saturdays, every week; samedi alone = this Saturday. Faire du + sport: faire du vélo, du tennis, de la natation.
en.literal: the Saturday, I do often some bike

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: C’est vrai ? Moi aussi, je suis fan de vélo !

forms.text: C’est vrai ? Moi aussi, je suis fan de vélo !

en.meaning: Really? Me too, I'm a big cycling fan!
en.note: Être fan de = to be a big fan of, very common among younger French speakers. Moi aussi = me too; moi non plus = me neither.
en.literal: it is true? me also, I am fan of bike

expressions.pronunciationNote: Fan is said as in English. Vrai: vreh.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: J’adore rouler sur les quais du Rhône.

forms.text: J’adore rouler sur les quais du Rhône.

en.meaning: I love riding along the banks of the Rhône.
en.note: Adorer + infinitive = to love doing. Cyclists and drivers say rouler (to roll) for riding. Lyon's riverbanks, les quais, have long car-free paths.
en.literal: I adore to-roll on the quays of-the Rhône

expressions.pronunciationNote: Rouler: roo-LAY. Quais: kay. Rhône: rohn.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Par contre, je déteste monter à la Croix-Rousse !

forms.text: Par contre, je déteste monter à la Croix-Rousse !

en.meaning: On the other hand, I hate riding up to the Croix-Rousse!
en.note: Par contre = on the other hand. The Croix-Rousse is the steep hill just north of the city centre, dreaded by Lyon's cyclists. Détester + infinitive = to hate doing.
en.literal: by against, I detest to-climb to the Cross-Red

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Ha ha, moi aussi ! Et le soir, plutôt films ou livres ?

forms.text: Ha ha, moi aussi ! Et le soir, plutôt films ou livres ?

en.meaning: Ha ha, me too! And in the evening, films or books?
en.note: Plutôt X ou Y ? (rather X or Y?) is the quick way to ask about someone's tastes, with no verb at all.
en.literal: ha ha, me also! and the evening, rather films or books

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je préfère les films, surtout en VO.

forms.text: Je préfère les films, surtout en VO.

en.meaning: I prefer films, especially in the original language.
en.note: En VO (version originale) = in the original language with subtitles; en VF = dubbed into French. Préférer takes the article: je préfère les films.
en.literal: I prefer the films, above-all in OV

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Et toi, tu préfères quoi ?

forms.text: Et toi, tu préfères quoi ?

en.meaning: What about you, which do you prefer?
en.note: Et toi ? hands the question back; to someone you say vous to: et vous ?
en.literal: and you, you prefer what

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Moi, les livres ! Je lis tous les soirs dans le tram.

forms.text: Moi, les livres ! Je lis tous les soirs dans le tram.

en.meaning: Books, for me! I read every evening on the tram.
en.note: Starting with moi puts the stress on 'me', the way English does with the voice. Tous les soirs = every evening.
en.literal: me, the books! I read all the evenings in the tram

expressions.pronunciationNote: Lis: lee. Tous les soirs: too lay SWAHR.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: On fait une balade à vélo dimanche ?

forms.text: On fait une balade à vélo dimanche ?

en.meaning: Shall we go for a bike ride on Sunday?
en.note: Une balade = a ride or a walk for pleasure: une balade à pied, à vélo, en bateau. On fait… ? is how friends suggest a plan.
en.literal: one does a ride at bike Sunday

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: J’aime mieux les films que les livres.

forms.text: J’aime mieux les films que les livres.

en.meaning: I like films better than books.
en.note: Aimer mieux X que Y = to like X better than Y, a little more relaxed than préférer.
en.literal: I love better the films than the books

sceneNotes.en: A small café near Place des Terreaux; Gérard, the owner, was born in Lyon and knows the places tourists never find.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Pardon, monsieur, je peux vous demander un conseil ?

forms.text: Pardon, monsieur, je peux vous demander un conseil ?

en.meaning: Excuse me, sir, can I ask you for some advice?
en.note: Pardon works like 'excuse me' to get someone's attention. Un conseil = a piece of advice; the plural des conseils is common.
en.literal: pardon, sir, I can you ask an advice

expressions.pronunciationNote: Monsieur: muh-SYUH. Conseil: kon-SAY, ending in a light y.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Qu’est-ce qu’il faut voir à Lyon, d’après vous ?

forms.text: Qu’est-ce qu’il faut voir à Lyon, d’après vous ?

en.meaning: What should I see in Lyon, in your opinion?
en.note: Il faut + infinitive = one must, you have to: il faut voir, il faut goûter. D’après vous = in your opinion.
en.literal: what is-it that it is-needed to-see at Lyon, from-after you

expressions.pronunciationNote: Il faut: eel FOH. D’après: dah-PREH.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Allez au marché de la Croix-Rousse, un dimanche matin.

forms.text: Allez au marché de la Croix-Rousse, un dimanche matin.

en.meaning: Go to the Croix-Rousse market on a Sunday morning.
en.note: The Croix-Rousse market stretches along the boulevard every morning except Monday; Sunday is its liveliest day.
en.literal: go to-the market of the Cross-Red, a Sunday morning

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Ah bon ? Pourquoi celui-là ?

forms.text: Ah bon ? Pourquoi celui-là ?

en.meaning: Really? Why that one?
en.note: Celui-là = that one, for a masculine noun (le marché); celle-là for a feminine one.
en.literal: ah good? why that-one-there

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: C’est le marché des Lyonnais, pas des touristes !

forms.text: C’est le marché des Lyonnais, pas des touristes !

en.meaning: It's where the people of Lyon shop, not the tourists!
en.note: Les Lyonnais = the people of Lyon. In quick speech pas alone can negate a single word: pas des touristes.
en.literal: it is the market of-the Lyonnais, not of-the tourists

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Il est ouvert tous les jours ?

forms.text: Il est ouvert tous les jours ?

en.meaning: Is it open every day?
en.note: Ouvert / fermé = open / closed. Many French shops and markets close on Sunday afternoon or on Monday, so it is always worth asking.
en.literal: it is open all the days

expressions.pronunciationNote: Ouvert: oo-VAIR, silent t. Tous les jours: too lay ZHOOR.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Tous les matins, sauf le lundi.

forms.text: Tous les matins, sauf le lundi.

en.meaning: Every morning, except Mondays.
en.note: Sauf = except. Le lundi with le = on Mondays, every week.
en.literal: all the mornings, except the Monday

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Et comment est-ce qu’on y va, d’ici ?

forms.text: Et comment est-ce qu’on y va, d’ici ?

en.meaning: And how do you get there from here?
en.note: Y = there: on y va = one goes there. Est-ce que turns a statement into a question without changing the word order.
en.literal: and how is-it that one there goes, from-here

expressions.pronunciationNote: Comment est-ce qu’on y va: ko-mahn ess-kon-nee VAH.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: C’est loin, à pied ?

forms.text: C’est loin, à pied ?

en.meaning: Is it far on foot?
en.note: À pied = on foot; en métro = by metro, en bus = by bus.
en.literal: it is far, at foot

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Non, mais ça monte ! Prenez le métro C, c’est deux arrêts.

forms.text: Non, mais ça monte ! Prenez le métro C, c’est deux arrêts.

en.meaning: No, but it's uphill! Take metro line C, it's two stops.
en.note: Ça monte = it's uphill. Metro line C climbs from Hôtel de Ville up to Croix-Rousse; it is a rack railway, built for the steep slope.
en.literal: no, but that climbs! take the metro C, it is two stops

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Merci beaucoup pour vos conseils !

forms.text: Merci beaucoup pour vos conseils !

en.meaning: Thanks a lot for your advice!
en.note: Merci pour + noun: merci pour vos conseils, merci pour tout. Advice is countable in French, so it is plural here.
en.literal: thanks much for your advices

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Vous me conseillez quoi, pour ce week-end ?

forms.text: Vous me conseillez quoi, pour ce week-end ?

en.meaning: What would you recommend for this weekend?
en.note: Conseiller quelque chose à quelqu’un = to recommend something to someone. Quoi at the end sounds relaxed but stays polite with vous.
en.literal: you to-me advise what, for this weekend

sceneNotes.en: Over a drink on a terrace by the Saône, your friend Hugo, who grew up in a Beaujolais village, insists the countryside beats the city.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Franchement, la campagne, c’est mieux que la ville !

forms.text: Franchement, la campagne, c’est mieux que la ville !

en.meaning: Honestly, the countryside is better than the city!
en.note: Franchement (frankly) opens many opinions among friends. Mieux (better) is the everyday comparative of bien: c’est mieux que…
en.literal: frankly, the countryside, it is better than the town

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d’accord.

forms.text: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d’accord.

en.meaning: I don't quite agree.
en.note: Pas tout à fait = not quite: a soft way to disagree. Plain je ne suis pas d’accord is fine too, just blunter.
en.literal: I not am not all at made of agreement

expressions.pronunciationNote: Tout à fait: too-tah-FEH; the t of tout links to à.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Moi, je trouve la ville plus pratique.

forms.text: Moi, je trouve la ville plus pratique.

en.meaning: Personally, I find the city more convenient.
en.note: Je trouve (I find) is the most common way to give an opinion: je trouve ça cher. False friend: pratique means convenient, handy, not only 'practical'.
en.literal: me, I find the town more practical

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Ah bon ? Et pourquoi ?

forms.text: Ah bon ? Et pourquoi ?

en.meaning: Oh really? Why's that?
en.note: Ah bon ? shows surprise, like 'oh, really?', and invites a reason.
en.literal: ah good? and why

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Parce qu’on peut tout faire à pied ou en métro.

forms.text: Parce qu’on peut tout faire à pied ou en métro.

en.meaning: Because you can do everything on foot or by metro.
en.note: Parce que (because) becomes parce qu’ before a vowel. On is the general 'you' here. Tout goes before the infinitive: tout faire.
en.literal: because that one can all to-do at foot or in metro

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Oui, mais en ville, les loyers sont beaucoup trop chers !

forms.text: Oui, mais en ville, les loyers sont beaucoup trop chers !

en.meaning: Yes, but in the city, rents are far too high!
en.note: Le loyer = the rent. Trop = too; beaucoup trop = far too. Rents in Lyon are among the highest in France outside Paris.
en.literal: yes, but in town, the rents are much too expensive

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Là, je suis d’accord avec toi.

forms.text: Là, je suis d’accord avec toi.

en.meaning: On that, I agree with you.
en.note: Là (there) = on that point. Être d’accord avec quelqu’un = to agree with someone; d’accord on its own means OK.
en.literal: there, I am of agreement with you

expressions.pronunciationNote: D’accord: dah-KOR. Avec toi: ah-vek TWAH.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Mais pour le travail, tu en penses quoi ?

forms.text: Mais pour le travail, tu en penses quoi ?

en.meaning: But what about work, what do you think?
en.note: Penser de = to think of (an opinion). En stands for 'of it': tu en penses quoi ? = what do you think of it?
en.literal: but for the work, you of-it think what

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: C’est vrai, c’est plus facile en ville. Un point pour toi !

forms.text: C’est vrai, c’est plus facile en ville. Un point pour toi !

en.meaning: True, it's easier in the city. A point to you!
en.note: Un point pour toi ! = one point to you: a playful way to give in during a friendly argument.
en.literal: it is true, it is more easy in town. a point for you

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: À mon avis, la ville, c’est mieux.

forms.text: À mon avis, la ville, c’est mieux.

en.meaning: In my opinion, the city is better.
en.note: À mon avis = in my opinion. False friend: un avis is an opinion; a piece of advice is un conseil.
en.literal: at my opinion, the town, it is better

sceneNotes.en: Camille, your friend since your first days in Lyon, meets you for a coffee; you tell her how you got lost in the old town last night.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Tu sais quoi ? Hier soir, je me suis perdu !

forms.text: Tu sais quoi ? Hier soir, je me suis perdu !

en.meaning: Guess what? I got lost last night!
en.note: Se perdre (to get lost) takes être in the passé composé: je me suis perdu. A woman writes perdue; it sounds the same. Tu sais quoi ? = guess what?
en.literal: you know what? yesterday evening, I myself am lost

expressions.pronunciationNote: Hier: yair, one syllable. Perdu: pair-DÜ.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Perdu ? Comment ça ?

forms.text: Perdu ? Comment ça ?

en.meaning: Lost? What do you mean?
en.note: Comment ça ? = what do you mean? how so? Repeating a word with a rising voice asks for more.
en.literal: lost? how that

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: J’ai pris une traboule dans le Vieux-Lyon, et je suis sorti ailleurs.

forms.text: J’ai pris une traboule dans le Vieux-Lyon, et je suis sorti ailleurs.

en.meaning: I took a traboule in the old town and came out somewhere else.
en.note: Traboules are passages through buildings and courtyards, a Lyon speciality. Prendre → j’ai pris (with avoir); sortir → je suis sorti (with être; a woman writes sortie).
en.literal: I have taken a traboule in the Old-Lyon, and I am gone-out elsewhere

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Oh non ! Il était quelle heure ?

forms.text: Oh non ! Il était quelle heure ?

en.meaning: Oh no! What time was it?
en.note: Il était (it was) is the imperfect: it sets the scene in a story, while the passé composé tells what happened.
en.literal: oh no! it was what hour

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Il était minuit. Enfin, onze heures, je veux dire.

forms.text: Il était minuit. Enfin, onze heures, je veux dire.

en.meaning: It was midnight. Well, eleven, I mean.
en.note: Enfin (literally 'finally') also corrects what you have just said, like 'well'. Je veux dire = I mean.
en.literal: it was midnight. finally, eleven hours, I want to-say

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Heureusement, un monsieur m’a aidé.

forms.text: Heureusement, un monsieur m’a aidé.

en.meaning: Luckily, a man helped me.
en.note: Heureusement = luckily. M’a aidé = helped me: the object pronoun comes before avoir. Un monsieur is a polite way to say 'a man'.
en.literal: happily, a sir me has helped

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Ah, sympa ! Et qu’est-ce qu’il t’a dit ?

forms.text: Ah, sympa ! Et qu’est-ce qu’il t’a dit ?

en.meaning: Oh, nice! And what did he say?
en.note: Sympa (short for sympathique) = nice, friendly. False friend: sympathique never means 'sympathetic'.
en.literal: ah, nice! and what is-it that he to-you has said

expressions.pronunciationNote: Sympa: san-PAH. Il t’a dit: eel tah DEE.

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Il connaissait un « shortcut ». Comment on dit ça en français ?

forms.text: Il connaissait un « shortcut ». Comment on dit ça en français ?

en.meaning: He knew a shortcut. How do you say that in French?
en.note: Comment on dit… en français ? is the question to keep asking. Connaître (to know a person or a place) → il connaissait, the imperfect.
en.literal: he knew a « shortcut ». how one says that in French

expressions.pronunciationNote: Connaissait: koh-neh-SEH. On dit: on DEE.

expressions.speaker: character
expressions.text: Un raccourci ! Tu as eu de la chance.

forms.text: Un raccourci ! Tu as eu de la chance.

en.meaning: A shortcut! You were lucky.
en.note: Un raccourci comes from court (short). False friend: avoir de la chance = to be lucky; 'a chance' is une occasion.
en.literal: a shortcut! you have had of the luck

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: La prochaine fois, je prendrai le métro !

forms.text: La prochaine fois, je prendrai le métro !

en.meaning: Next time, I'll take the metro!
en.note: Prendrai is the future of prendre: drop the final e of the infinitive and add -ai. La prochaine fois = next time.
en.literal: the next time, I will-take the metro

expressions.speaker: learner
expressions.text: Comment ça s’appelle, en français ?

forms.text: Comment ça s’appelle, en français ?

en.meaning: What's it called in French?
en.note: Ça s’appelle (it calls itself) = it's called: the same verb as je m’appelle. Point at the thing as you ask.
en.literal: how that itself calls, in French
